paper_title: An economy of scales: A selective review of obesity’s economic causes, consequences, and solutions

block_set.title: Abstract
block_set.sub_firstblock: Article history: Available online 14 August 2015

block_set.title: 1. Introduction
block_set.sub_firstblock: The prevalence of obesity has risen dramatically in the United States and most other economically developed countries in the past several decades (National Center for Health Statistics, 2014; OECD, 2014). Concern about the health risks, medical care costs, and other consequences of obesity has led to a host of policies and programs implemented by companies, school districts, and governments to prevent and reduce obesity. It has also resulted in a large body of economic research on the causes and consequences of obesity and on approaches to prevent and reduce obesity. The purpose of this article is to organize and synthesize what is known from this literature and to identify the most pressing needs and promising opportunities for future research.

block_set.title: 2. The economic causes of obesity
block_set.sub_firstblock: The first law of thermodynamics states that in a closed system energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be transformed. In the context of obesity, this implies that calories consumed must be either expended, excreted, or stored by the body as fat.

block_set.title: 2.1. The money price and time cost of food
block_set.sub_firstblock: In the past several decades, the real prices of energy-dense foods (i.e. foods with a high number of calories per unit weight) have fallen relative to the prices of less energy-dense, nutritious foods. For example, between 1990 and 2007, the real price of a 2-L bottle of Coca Cola fell $3 4 . 9 \%$ and the real price of a 12-in. pizza at Pizza Hut fell $1 7 . 2 \%$ (Christian and Rashad, 2009) while the prices of fresh fruits and vegetables rose faster than inflation (Wendt and Todd, 2011; Sturm, 2005b). If these types of food are normal goods, then consumers likely responded to these price changes by increasing their consumption of energy-dense foods and decreasing their consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables. A large number of papers have regressed obesity or BMI on local food prices; the limitation of this approach is that variation in local food prices may be due to differences in demand over geography and changes in demand over time and thus the estimates of the impact of local food prices on weight may be biased.

block_set.title: 2.2. Food assistance programs
block_set.sub_firstblock: The U.S. has many government programs that subsidize food, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the National School Lunch Program (NSLP), and the School Breakfast Program (SBP). Although they were originally designed to reduce hunger and under-nutrition, they may have the unintended consequence of increasing obesity for certain individuals. For example, benefits in the SNAP program can be spent on the full range of groceries; only prepared food (such as hot rotisserie chicken or sandwiches) and alcohol are excluded, which means that the program subsidizes energy-dense (as well as other) groceries. For example, grocery store scanner data suggest that SNAP pays for roughly $\$ 2$ billion worth of sugar-sweetened beverages annually (Andreyeva et al., 2012).

block_set.title: 2.3. Income
block_set.sub_firstblock: In general, there is a robust negative correlation between weight and income among women but not men; i.e. higher-income women are less likely to be obese (Sobal and Stunkard, 1989; McLaren, 2007). For example, in the NHANES data for 2005–2008, the prevalence of obesity among adult women was $2 9 . 0 \%$ for women living in a household with a poverty-to-income ratio (PIR) greater than $3 5 0 \%$ but $4 2 . 0 \%$ for those living in a household with a PIR of less than $1 3 0 \%$ (Ogden et al., 2010).

block_set.title: 2.4. Education
block_set.sub_firstblock: One of the most consistent findings in health economics is that those with higher education tend to be in better health (see, e.g. Grossman, 2006), and obesity is no exception. In the NHANES data for 2005–2008, the prevalence of adult obesity is $2 3 . 4 \%$ for women with a college degree and $4 2 . 1 \%$ for women who are high school dropouts (Ogden et al., 2010). For men, the correlation is weaker; the prevalence of obesity is $2 7 . 4 \%$ for men with a college degree compared to $3 2 . 1 \%$ for men who are high school dropouts (Ibid).

block_set.title: 2.5. Macroeconomic conditions
block_set.sub_firstblock: The macroeconomy is another possible contributor to obesity. When the unemployment rate is high many people experience declines in income and employment. This decrease in labor market opportunities can have both substitution and income effects. The substitution effect is relatively straightforward: when wages are low so is the opportunity cost of time, and thus recessions may lead to more time-intensive investments in health such as physical activity and cooking from scratch. The income effect on health is ambiguous. Lower income could lead to a decrease in calorie consumption (e.g. cooking rice and beans at home instead of buying fast food) or an increase in calories (e.g. substituting energy-dense, low nutrient foods for more expensive fresh fruits and vegetables). Even conditional on income and employment, economic downturns could affect health by increasing stress, taking up mental bandwidth and reducing self-control or willpower (Mani et al., 2013), with deleterious consequences for diet and physical activity (e.g. De Vriendt et al., 2009). Stress also leads to the release of the hormone cortisol, which has complex effects but can increase appetite (especially for energy-dense foods), insulin resistance, and increased abdominal fat accumulation (e.g. Bjorntorp, 1997).

block_set.title: 2.6. Peer and neighborhood effects
block_set.sub_firstblock: Peers may influence diet or physical activity through bandwagon effects; it may be more enjoyable to eat, diet, or exercise when one’s peers are doing the same. Identifying peer effects is notoriously difficult because individuals tend to associate with people like themselves and peers tend to have similar environmental influences (Manski, 1993). Yakusheva et al. (2014) identify peer effects by exploiting the randomization of freshman roommates at two universities. Following the literature that defines the roommate receiving influence as the ego and the roommate doing the influencing as the alter, they estimate the influence of the alter’s weight at baseline (just before freshman year) on the change in weight of the ego during freshman year; the model also controls for a complete set of indicator variables for all possible combinations of the factors used by the administration to make roommate assignments (such as preferred area of campus and smoking status). Results from these models are consistent with a significant positive peer effect on weight for females; for every standard deviation increase in the baseline weight of the alter, the ego gains an additional 0.8 pounds during freshman year (compared to an average freshman year weight gain of 2.4 pounds). They cannot reject the null hypothesis of no peer effects on weight for males. The authors explore heterogeneity in these peer effects, and find that the females who are most influenced by their roommates are those in the lowest and highest quartiles of the baseline weight distribution. They also find that alters have the greatest effect on egos when the alter is higher in the social hierarchy; specifically, when the alter is lighter, comes from a higher-SES household, or is more sexually experienced than the ego. There are no such differences for males.

block_set.title: 3. The economic consequences of obesity
block_set.sub_firstblock: The economic consequences of obesity include worse labor market outcomes, such as lower wages and a lower probability of employment, and higher medical care costs. When studying the causes of obesity, there is often the potential to conduct randomized experiments: e.g. to randomize children into a preschool program in order to measure the impact of education on obesity or to randomize college roommates in order to test for peer effects in weight. That is more difficult when obesity is the endogenous regressor rather than the outcome. It would, obviously, be unethical to force a subject randomized to the treatment group to become obese so one could study the resulting increase in medical care costs. It is possible to randomly assign overweight individuals interested in weight loss to a weight loss treatment, but the effect measured would reflect not just the weight change but also the method of achieving it (such as bariatric surgery or increased time spent physically active) which could have a direct impact on the outcome. Due to the challenges of experimentally manipulating individuals’ weights, the literature on the economic consequences of obesity has relied solely on natural experiments for identification.

block_set.title: 3.1. Wages
block_set.sub_firstblock: A large literature has estimated the effect of weight or obesity on wages (see Averett, 2011, for a review). Cawley (2004) exploits the heritable component of weight by using the BMI of an adult biological sibling as an instrument for the BMI of the respondent. This instrument has the advantage of being powerful; twin studies indicate very high levels of heritability for BMI, up to $7 0 \mathrm { - } 8 0 \%$ (Farooqi and O’Rahilly, 2007; Pietilainen, 2014). The potential threat to validity is that the genes that affect obesity may also affect other things correlated with the error term in the wage equation. One might also be concerned about the possibility that a shared household environment makes biological relatives similar in weight and could be correlated with outcomes, but the preponderance of evidence suggests that any shared household environment effect on weight is so small as to be undetectable (see the review in Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012); consistent with this, the weight of nonbiological relatives (e.g. stepchildren or adopted children) are not significant predictors of respondent weight in the first stage of IV (Cawley, 2004; Lindeboom et al., 2010; Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012). Estimating IV models using data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, 1979 Cohort, for 1981–2000, Cawley (2004) finds that the effect of weight on wages varies by race and gender, with the greatest impact on white females, for whom an additional 10 pounds lowers wages by $2 . 8 \%$ .

block_set.title: 3.2. Employment
block_set.sub_firstblock: Others have examined the effect of obesity on employment. Lindeboom et al. (2010) examine data from the British National Child Development Study, which consists of 17,000 individuals born in Great Britain in one week in 1958, and records employment at ages 33 and 42 years. They observe large differences in the probability of employment between obese and non-obese men and women, but when they estimate IV models that use parental obesity status as an instrument for respondent weight, they cannot reject the null hypothesis that obesity has no effect on employment. Another study to test for an impact of obesity on employment in the UK (Morris, 2007) instrumented for respondent obesity using the prevalence of obesity in the local health authority, but this may be invalid if respondents sort into neighborhoods based on unobserved demand (e.g. for proximity to restaurants or exercise opportunities).

block_set.title: 3.3. Medical care costs
block_set.sub_firstblock: Given the strong link between obesity and heart disease, cancer, and Type II diabetes, another likely economic consequence of obesity is elevated medical care costs. Cawley and Meyerhoefer (2012) and Cawley et al. (2015) estimate IV two-part models of medical expenditures using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey. The IV model exploits the heritable component of weight by instrumenting for respondent obesity using the BMI and BMI squared of a biological child. The models indicate that in 2010 obesity raised annual medical care costs by $\$ 3508$ (in 2010 dollars); however, the effects of BMI on medical care costs are highly non-linear (Cawley et al., 2015). For men, medical care costs are Ushaped in BMI, with much higher expenditures for those who are underweight or morbidly obese. For women, medical care costs are J-shaped in BMI with a large increase in medical care costs with BMI among those who are morbidly obese. For both men and women, predicted medical care costs for individuals just over the threshold of obesity are not significantly higher than those of healthy weight individuals. However, costs rise exponentially in the morbidly obese range $\left( \mathsf { B M I } \ge 3 5 \right)$ , which indicates that the greatest potential savings may come from facilitating weight loss in that group or preventing additional weight gain among obese individuals. This pattern of medical care expenditures matches that of mortality risk: flat throughout the overweight and obese class 1 range, rising with BMI in the morbidly obese range; see Flegal et al. (2013). Assuming that the estimates from the regression sample of adults with biological children in the household generalize to the full population of non-institutionalized adults, the IV model implies that the total direct medical care costs of obesity for the U.S. population of adults was $\$ 315.8$ billion in 2010, which equaled $2 7 . 5 \%$ of the health expenditures for non-institutionalized U.S. adults (Cawley et al., 2015).

block_set.title: 4. The negative externalities of obesity
block_set.sub_firstblock: Obesity imposes large external costs, which likely decrease social welfare. Third-party payers cover most of the costs of obesity related illness; e.g. in 2005, $8 8 . 2 \%$ of the total medical care costs of obesity in the U.S. were paid by health insurance companies, Medicare, and Medicaid (Cawley and Meyerhoefer, 2012). Ultimately, many of these costs of obesity were paid by non-obese individuals. In group health insurance, the premium paid by each individual does not depend upon his or her weight; as a result, healthy-weight individuals subsidize the health care costs of obese individuals. The same is true for Medicare, which is funded by payroll taxes, and Medicaid, which is funded with general revenues; in public health insurance programs, healthy-weight individuals subsidize the medical care costs of obese individuals.

block_set.title: 5. Policies to internalize the external costs of obesity
block_set.sub_firstblock: There are several possible approaches to internalizing the external costs of obesity. The most direct would be to tax excess body fat by an amount equal to its marginal external cost. No country has yet implemented such a tax, perhaps because of concerns about discriminating against those with a genetic predisposition to fatness. However, Singapore implemented a program called “Trim and Fit” from 1992 to 2008 in which schoolchildren’s BMIs were measured and youths deemed overweight were assigned extra physical activity at school. There were no financial penalties for youths or their families but schools could be rewarded or punished based on progress toward goals. Singapore’s health ministry reported that the prevalence of youth obesity declined as a result (Toh et al., 2002) but it is not clear whether the intervention was rigorously evaluated.

block_set.title: 5.1. Raising health insurance premia
block_set.sub_firstblock: One could argue that the health care externality of obesity is due to a failure in the pricing of health insurance; specifically, that individual premia are not adjusted to reflect the expected medical care costs associated with the individual’s weight. Therefore, one way to eliminate the health care externality of obesity is to charge sufficiently higher premia to obese individuals. The U.S. has recently moved to provide insurers with greater flexibility to do this; the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010 (ACA) allows group health insurers to offer rewards in wellness programs for weight loss that equal up to $3 0 \%$ of the total individual premium (i.e. the sum of the premia paid by the individual and the employer). Insurers are given considerable latitude in designing these incentives; they can be rewards or penalties, and can take the form of modified premiums, copays, or deductibles.

block_set.title: 5.2. Financial rewards for weight loss
block_set.sub_firstblock: A related approach is to offer obese individuals financial rewards for weight loss outside of the health insurance system. These could be set based on the expected medical care savings (and other reductions in marginal external costs); e.g. they might be negligible for those in the overweight and class 1 obese range, but substantial for those with class 2 or class 3 obesity.

block_set.title: 5.3. Taxes on energy-dense foods
block_set.sub_firstblock: Financial rewards for weight loss have a mixed record of effectiveness (Cawley and Price, 2013; Department of the Treasury, Department of Labor, and Department of Health and Human Services, 2013; Horwitz et al., 2013; Jeffery, 2012). Some studies have found substantial weight loss in such programs. For example, Volpp et al. (2008) find that offering a lottery with an expected daily value of \$3 results in an average weight loss of 9.2 pounds relative to the control group after 16 weeks. In contrast, several studies have found no detectable weight loss from rewards that consisted of: $\$ 7-14$ per percentage point of weight lost (Finkelstein et al., 2007), $\$ 100$ per month for achieving weight loss goals (Kullgren et al., 2013), or $\$ 3-5$ per quarter for each percentage point of baseline weight lost (Cawley and Price, 2013). An important limitation of this research is that the participants are volunteers interested in weight loss; thus, it is unknown how effective incentives would be for people who do not wish to lose weight (Jeffery, 2012). Another complication is that attrition in such programs can be substantial, despite the fact that all participants are volunteers being paid to achieve their own goals; e.g. the workplace wellness program studied by Cawley and Price (2013) experienced attrition of $5 4 . 9 \%$ after 3 months and $7 5 . 8 \%$ after 12 months.

block_set.title: 5.4. Subsidies for healthy food
block_set.sub_firstblock: An alternative to taxing energy-dense, non-nutritious foods is to subsidize nutritious, less energy-dense foods. A large number of studies have experimentally subsidized the prices of healthy foods, sometimes by very large amounts; see the review in Epstein et al. (2012). Some take place in laboratory settings with questionable generalizability, but others have taken place in cafeterias or vending machines in the field. For example, subsidizing fruit and salads in university and high school cafeterias by $5 0 \%$ resulted in a tripling to quadrupling of sales (Jeffery et al., 1994; French et al., 1997); however, these price reductions were combined with other interventions such as signs and increased diversity of healthy food choices, so that increase in demand cannot be attributed solely to the price change. Moreover, the behavior change did not result in lasting healthier habits; sales fell back to baseline levels after the removal of the subsidy.

block_set.title: 5.5. Subsidies for physical activity
block_set.sub_firstblock: Taxpayers subsidize the physical activity of youth through sports teams and physical education (PE) classes in public schools. Several organizations, such as the Centers for Disease Control, American Academy of Pediatrics, and Institute of Medicine, have called for increases in PE to prevent and reduce youth obesity. To estimate the impact of PE on the physical activity and weight of high school students, Cawley et al. (2007) instrument for the amount of time that high school students spend in PE using state PE requirements, while controlling for state socioeconomic characteristics and education spending to reduce the risks of policy endogeneity. IV models, estimated using data from the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System, indicate that increasing PE time increases physical activity among high school girls (but not boys) but has no detectable effect on BMI or the probability of obesity for either sex.

block_set.title: 6. Policies to correct other market failures
block_set.sub_firstblock: Internalizing external costs is not the only economic rationale for government intervention. Economists also recognize a role for government policies to address the market failure of imperfect information, help consumers who have time-inconsistent preferences, or protect those who act irrationally.

block_set.title: 6.1. Imperfect information
block_set.sub_firstblock: Consumers often lack important information about calories and nutrients at the point of food purchase and consumption. One policy that addresses this market failure is the requirement that restaurants post calorie counts and other nutrition information on their menus and menu boards. This policy was enacted by several municipalities (such as New York City and King County, Washington) and a nationwide menu labeling law was included in the ACA of 2010.

block_set.title: 6.2. Time-inconsistent preferences
block_set.sub_firstblock: Nearly half of Americans are actively trying to lose weight (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2008), and roughly $\$ 60$ billion is spent annually on diet and weight loss products (Marketdata, 2014). However, the vast majority of weight loss attempts fail, and even among those who initially succeed in losing weight, most return to their baseline weight within three to five years (e.g. Crawford et al., 2000; Jones-Corneille et al., 2011). The basic problem is that eating is enjoyable and dieting and exercise are not (at least at first); as a result, an obese individual trying to lose weight experiences high costs early on, but virtually all of the benefits (such as better health) are in the distant future.

block_set.title: 6.3. Irrational behavior
block_set.sub_firstblock: Another economic rationale for government intervention is to protect consumers who are incapable of acting in their own interest. This is a dangerous rationale to invoke, however, because irrationality is in the eye of the beholder and it can be a slippery slope to paternalism. However, there is general agreement that children are not able to foresee the full consequences of their actions. block_set.title: 7. The economics of obesity: a research agenda
block_set.sub_firstblock: This section proposes a research agenda for the economics of obesity.

block_set.title: 7.1. Obesity measurement
block_set.sub_firstblock: An important priority that relates to every aspect of research on this subject is the need for social science datasets to collect higherquality data: measurements rather than self-reports of weight and height, plus more accurate measures of fatness (Burkhauser and Cawley, 2009). Ideally, this would include body composition – fat and lean mass – measured by state-of-the-art technology (the NHANES currently uses Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry), and would include information not just on quantity of fat mass but also its location in the body. Even measured waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio, though less accurate, would be of value because they reflect central adiposity.

block_set.title: 7.2. Causes of obesity
block_set.sub_firstblock: The previous research on certain economic causes of obesity (e.g. education and the macroeconomy) has found mixed results. To some extent, the heterogeneous and contradictory findings may be due to differences in data and the subgroups among whom the Local Average Treatment Effect is measured. Future research should seek to resolve these discrepancies and estimate effects for subgroups of particular interest, such as children and the economically vulnerable.

block_set.title: 7.3. Genetic markers
block_set.sub_firstblock: Genes are a particularly interesting natural experiment that epidemiologists refer to as Mendellian Randomization (Davey Smith and Ebrahim, 2005). Genes are an appealing source of variation because they are beyond the individual’s control and long precede the outcome – they are determined even before birth. However, to date it has proven challenging to use individual genes as instruments for obesity (Cawley et al., 2011). They tend not to be powerful instruments because, although genetic factors play an important role in obesity (Farooqi and O’Rahilly, 2007; Pietilainen, 2014) individual genes tend to have little independent influence on weight and geneticists’ understanding of those processes are far from complete; all known genetic polymorphisms combined explain less than $2 \%$ of the variance in obesity (Winter et al., 2013). There have also been challenges to validity; some studies have used as instruments alleles that, in addition to being only very weakly correlated with obesity, are associated with other risky behaviors and thus are likely to affect the outcome through channels other than obesity (see the discussion in Cawley et al., 2011). One of the strongest papers in this area is Von Hinke Kessler Scholder et al. (2012), which instruments for fat mass using the genetic marker FTO, which is highly correlated with fatness and does not seem to have the problems with validity that plagued genetic instruments used in earlier studies. As genetic research on obesity progresses, the suitability of specific genes as instruments in specific circumstances should become clearer.

block_set.title: 7.4. Obesity and risky behaviors
block_set.sub_firstblock: Another important direction for future research is to better investigate the extent to which the causes and consequences of obesity are similar to those for risky behaviors such as heavy or binge drinking, use of narcotics, abuse of prescription drugs, smoking, and unprotected sex. All involve dramatic tradeoffs between immediate gratification and future health, and thus rates of time discount and the extent of risk aversion are relevant (Cawley and Ruhm, 2012). For each, time-inconsistent preferences could have a substantial impact on behavior, and there is a potential conflict between the deliberative prefrontal cortex and the impulsive limbic system (Ibid). If risky behaviors had the same causes, one would expect to see a high correlation between them, but Cutler and Glaeser (2005) find that correlations across risky behaviors (both participation and changes in participation) tend to be below $1 0 \%$ . Most studies of risky behaviors tend to focus on just one or a few of them, and the field would benefit from research testing for similarities and differences between a large number of risky behaviors.

block_set.title: 7.5. Consequences of obesity
block_set.sub_firstblock: Most of the causal estimates of the consequences of obesity are based on the use of the weight of a biological relative as an instrument; future research should seek to identify additional natural experiments for weight. One could also exploit randomized controlled trials of weight loss interventions to examine the effect of weight loss on economic outcomes, although samples may be small and the estimates may reflect not only the effect of weight loss but also that of the method of achieving it (e.g. bariatric surgery may temporarily affect productivity and exercise programs may have direct health benefits).

block_set.title: 7.6. Effective interventions
block_set.sub_firstblock: An important contribution can be made by evaluating the effectiveness of policies and interventions that seek to prevent or reduce obesity, and then using that information to improve them. The ACA of 2010 alone enacted several new programs: the nationwide menu labeling law, increased flexibility for workplace wellness programs to offer financial rewards for weight loss, awards to states to provide incentives for healthy behavior among beneficiaries of Medicaid and Medicare, and community transformation grants to promote healthier lifestyles.

block_set.title: 7.7. Explaining disparities and heterogeneity in effects
block_set.sub_firstblock: Investigating differences among different population subgroups, and using that information to tailor policies to those subgroups, is another priority. One important unanswered question about obesity is: why does it vary so much by race and ethnicity? In the NHANES data for 2011–2012, the prevalence of obesity was $1 0 . 8 \%$ among Asian-Americans, $3 2 . 6 \%$ among non-Hispanic whites, $4 2 . 5 \%$ among Hispanics, and $4 7 . 8 \%$ among non-Hispanic blacks (Ogden et al., 2014). Some of this difference is due to the fact that BMI ignores differences in body composition, and as a result BMI understates obesity in Asian-Americans (Jih et al., 2014) and overstates it in African-Americans (Burkhauser and Cawley, 2008). Within most race/ethnic groups, the prevalence of obesity is similar for women and men, but this is not true for African-Americans, among whom the prevalence of obesity is much higher among women $( 5 6 . 6 \% )$ than men $( 3 7 . 1 \% )$ (Ogden et al., 2014). Explaining these large disparities represents an intriguing direction for future research.

block_set.title: 7.8. Behavioral economics approaches
block_set.sub_firstblock: The terms “behavioral economics” and “nudge” have been applied quite broadly, to include even very neoclassical approaches such as altering time costs, offering incentives, providing information, and harnessing peer effects. Clarity about which approaches are consistent with neoclassical economics and which are implied only by behavioral economics would be helpful.

block_set.title: 7.9. Cost effectiveness analysis
block_set.sub_firstblock: Another important priority is to assess the cost-effectiveness of existing programs and policies. In order to achieve the greatest increase in social welfare from a given budget devoted to obesity prevention, money should be allocated to programs based on their cost effectiveness. Studies have calculated the cost-effectiveness of both surgical and pharmaceutical treatment of obesity (e.g. Michaud et al., 2012) as well as many prevention programs (see Lehnert et al., 2012; Roux, 2011, for reviews), but for many programs not only the cost-effectiveness but even the effectiveness is unknown. The ACE (Assessing Cost Effectiveness) Obesity America project seeks to use a consistent methodology to measure the cost effectiveness of a wide range of interventions, and builds on a similarly ambitious program conducted in Australia (see Carter et al., 2009). Given the number of candidate interventions to be evaluated, there remain many opportunities to conduct costeffectiveness analyses of obesity policies and interventions, and evaluations of new programs designed to treat or prevent obesity should include a CEA component.

block_set.title: 8. Conclusion
block_set.sub_firstblock: The large literature on the economics of obesity indicates that numerous economic variables, such as food prices, the time cost of food acquisition, income, education, the macroeconomy, and peer behaviors, may have modest effects on weight and obesity. The magnitude, and sometimes the sign, of these effects vary by subgroup (e.g. gender, race, age, and income). There appears to be no single dominant economic cause of obesity; instead, a wide variety of factors may each contribute a small amount, and different economic variables may be relevant for different groups.
